findings.where: A-UVM-6, Push Further, "### Expert: configuring `compare()` for a scoreboard", line 1446; I-UVM-4, compare() section line 205 and "### Expert: Where the threshold lives..." line 864
findings.quotes: A-UVM-6: "So a portable scoreboard calls `set_threshold(0)` before each `compare()`". I-UVM-4: "A literally conforming library would therefore undo `cmp.set_threshold(0)` on every `compare()`" and "The robust pattern is the Make It Work `scb_comparer`, whose `flush()` calls `super.flush()` and re-applies the threshold."
findings.problem: The two lessons give different portable fixes, and A-UVM-6's does not work. A-UVM-6's own sentence just before it says that compare() flushes the comparer first and that a flush restores the threshold to 1. So a set_threshold(0) made before compare() is undone inside compare(). I-UVM-4 says exactly that and teaches the working fix: a comparer subclass that re-applies the threshold in flush(). A learner who reads I-UVM-4 and then A-UVM-6 meets two different 'portable' recipes, and the later one is wrong.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §5.3.9.1 a) (compare calls flush when the active object depth is 0); §16.3.6 ("since the last call to flush ... get_threshold shall return 1")
findings.fix: In A-UVM-6 line 1446, replace the sentence with: "So calling `set_threshold(0)` before `compare()` does not help: the flush inside `compare()` undoes it. A portable scoreboard uses a comparer subclass whose `flush()` calls `super.flush()` and re-applies the threshold ([I-UVM-4](/curriculum/T2_Intermediate/I-UVM-4_UVM_Policy_Classes/index), Make It Work `scb_comparer`). In uvm-core 2020.3.1, `flush()` keeps the threshold, so setting it once in `build_phase` is enough there."

findings.where: placementQuizData.ts question 'foundations-always-block' (prompt and rationale); F2C index.mdx lines 71 and 148
findings.quotes: Quiz: "guarantees a combinational sensitivity list without accidentally inferring latches" and rationale "emits errors when latches sneak in". F2C: "Tools *should* also warn when an `always_comb` body infers a latch ... findings.problem: The quiz tells the learner that always_comb guarantees no latch and that tools must give an error. A practitioner who answers correctly is shown a rationale that contradicts the lesson.

Replace the rationale with: "always_comb infers its sensitivity from what the body reads and asks tools to warn about latched behaviour (§9.2.2.2); a path that leaves an output unassigned still infers a latch, so assign every output at the top of the block." findings.where: F4C lines 598, 643, 647, 649 (heading 'Reset stays outside the clocking block') vs A-UVM-9 lines 96, 448-452, 879-886; I-SV-4C 690/702; I-SV-4B index 537/594; I-SV-4B local-variables 645/689; I-SV-7 984/1001; E-AI-1 695/725; I-UVM-3C 222/347
findings.quotes: F4C:647 "So reset stays a direct write." and F4C:649 "Releases it with a direct write between edges ... release it away from the active clock edge" | A-UVM-9:879 "a test drives a mid-test reset through cb, so it lands after an edge like every other drive"; I-SV-4C:702 "##2 cb.rst_n <= 1'b1;"
findings.problem: F4C builds its rule from an asynchronous reset that must change between edges, but its heading and its conclusion ('So reset stays a direct write') read as a general rule. Five later benches with asynchronous-reset DUTs (I-SV-4B index and local-variables, I-SV-4C, I-SV-7, E-AI-1) list rst_n as a clocking-block output and release it through cb at an edge. I-UVM-3C releases it with <= at the 15 ns edge. A-UVM-9 also asserts reset through cb. None of them says why that is acceptable or links back to F4C. A learner who has just been told 'reset stays a direct write' sees the opposite in every later bench. The code is deterministic: a release through cb lands in Re-NBA after the flops have captured with rst_n still 0 (§14.16, §4.5). A-UVM-9's DUT has a synchronous reset, so F4C's argument does not apply to it. What is inconsistent is the guidance, not a fact.
findings.fix: F4C: scope the rule. Retitle the section to 'Asserting an asynchronous reset stays outside the clocking block'. Add one sentence: releasing reset through a clocking block at an edge is deterministic in zero-delay RTL simulation, because the release lands in Re-NBA after that edge's capture (§14.16), and later benches do this; for a synchronous-reset DUT a clocking drive is the natural choice (A-UVM-9). Later lessons: add a one-line comment where rst_n is released through cb (I-SV-4B, I-SV-4C, I-SV-7, E-AI-1), and in A-UVM-9 near line 96, saying why a clocking drive is fine here (release only, or synchronous reset), with a link to F4C's reset section.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §14.16 (a drive between edges takes effect 'as if it were executed at the next clocking event'); §4.5 (Re-NBA updates are processed after the active set). Release timing is practice, which F4C itself labels as not a rule of the standard.

findings.quotes: F2C:194 "the report is held until the Observed region of that time slot ... so the time slot has settled"; F2C:800 "the result of the procedure's last run in the time slot matures in the Observed region" | F3B:1092 "Observed can run more than once per slot."; F3B:1148 "An observed deferred assertion can still report a glitch when Reactive code wakes the design and the block runs again in a later pass."
findings.problem: F2C tells learners that the time slot has settled when Observed is reached, and that only the procedure's last run in the slot is reported. Unique/priority violation reports work like observed deferred reports: they mature in Observed and can no longer be flushed (§12.4.2.1). F3B and I-SV-4A then teach that Observed can run again after Reactive code wakes the design, so a report that has matured can describe a value that is not the slot's final one. F2C's sentence is a fair Tier 1 simplification. But no later lesson connects the refinement back to unique/priority reports, so the 'settled' claim is never corrected for them.
findings.fix: F2C flow-control:194: replace 'so the time slot has settled' with 'so the design's own updates for this pass are done'. Add: 'Reactive-region code, such as a program block or a clocking-block drive, can wake the procedure again later in the slot; F3B shows when, and a report that has already matured stays.' F2C:800: replace 'the procedure's last run in the time slot' with 'the procedure's last run before the Observed region'. Optionally, in F3B's 'Loops still glitch' bullet (line 1148), add that unique/priority reports behave the same way (§12.4.2.1).
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §12.4.2.1 (violation reporting 'is deferred until the Observed region'; once a report matures it is reported and can no longer be flushed); §4.5 (the outer loop returns to Active and Observed after reactive-set activity); §16.4.1 (the same limit for observed deferred assertions).

I-SV-4B, citing the standard's finite-trace levels, says that state is "holds" and reserves "pending" for an open strong attempt. I-SV-4B says only that its visualizers show both cases as PENDING; it never tells the learner that I-SV-4A's term was a simplification. A learner meets the word with one meaning in 4A and then with a narrower, conflicting one in 4B.

findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §16.12.21: Pending means "Future obligations have not been met"; Annex F.5.3.2 gives "Holds (but does not hold strongly)" for a weak match that is not yet complete. §16.12.2 makes the sequence weak in assert property.

findings.where: I-UVM-1B index.mdx line 392 (the 'An unknown name returns null' bullet); I-SV-1 polymorphism-pitfalls.mdx lines 936-938 (the 'casting a null handle' interview question); B-APB-1 index.mdx line 1524 agrees with I-SV-1
findings.quotes: I-UVM-1B: "`$cast` of a null handle succeeds, so the cast alone does not catch it." | I-SV-1 Polymorphism Pitfalls: "§8.16 guarantees success only for the literal constant null. A variable that holds null is not spelled out." (it marks 'It always succeeds, because $cast of null succeeds' as the wrong answer)
findings.problem: Two lessons give opposite answers to the same question. I-UVM-1B has `obj` declared `uvm_object` and holding null, and states as fact that `$cast(seq, obj)` succeeds. I-SV-1 marks exactly that belief as a misconception in its interview question, and B-APB-1 also says the standard is not explicit and tools differ. A learner who takes the route I-SV-1, then I-UVM-1B is told a rule and then its opposite. I-UVM-1B's code is still safe, because it tests `obj == null` before the cast; only the reason it gives is wrong.
findings.fix: I-UVM-1B: replace the last sentence with: "Check for it, as the `if` above does. The standard does not say what `$cast` does with a handle variable that holds null (§8.16 guarantees success only for the literal `null`), and many simulators return 1, so the cast alone may not catch it. See [Polymorphism Pitfalls](/curriculum/T2_Intermediate/I-SV-1_OOP/polymorphism-pitfalls)." I-SV-1 Polymorphism Pitfalls and B-APB-1: no change needed; they match the standard.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §8.16 says `$cast` on class handles "succeeds in only three cases"; case 3 is "the literal constant null". Case 2 (source type is a superclass of the destination) needs a run-time check that the handle "refers to an object". The text does not settle a null-valued variable, which supports the I-SV-1 wording.

findings.where: F2A index.mdx line 382 (x in decisions) and line 1624 (Expert: X-propagation beyond the standard); debug.json line 244 (question debug-x-propagation, model_answer)
findings.quotes: F2A: "Operators that compute a value are **X-pessimistic**: they keep the `x` visible." | debug.json: "X-pessimism is the opposite problem. Gate models can produce X where real hardware is known (for example reconvergent logic such as `s & ~s` with `s` = X). That is a simulation artifact"
findings.problem: F2A presents X-pessimism as the desirable side, where the unknown stays visible. The interview bank defines it as an artifact: x where the real hardware value is known. The bank's own example, `s & ~s`, is also x in RTL under the operator tables F2A teaches, so the same behaviour is a virtue in one place and a defect in the other. A learner who meets both will hold two meanings of one term.
findings.fix: F2A index line 382: add half a sentence: "they keep the `x` visible, sometimes even where the real hardware value would be known (for example `s & ~s`), which is why the term is also used for false x at gate level." debug.json: no change needed; optionally add one line noting that RTL operators such as `&` and `+` are X-pessimistic in the same sense.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 does not define the terms X-optimism and X-pessimism, so the sources do not settle the definition. Tables 11-11 to 11-15 (§11.4.8) do settle the example: `x & ~x` evaluates to x.

findings.fix: Settled by IEEE 1800-2023 §3.12: the standard "does not normally specify requirements regarding the order of compilation for design elements"; the only exceptions are compilation units and packages (§26.3). findings.where: F4C 'Reset stays outside the clocking block', lines 643-649; I-UVM-3C lines 220-232 and 1241; A-UVM-9 lines 96 and 881-889 (rst_if drives rst_n through cb), 452 and 1442
findings.quotes: F4C:647-649: "So reset stays a direct write ... Releases it with a direct write between edges ... release it away from the active clock edge." | I-UVM-3C:231: "Reset is released with a nonblocking assignment at a rising edge" | A-UVM-9:882-889: "a test drives a mid-test reset through cb ... output rst_n; // default output skew 0: updated in Re-NBA"
findings.problem: F4C states as general practice that reset is a direct write, released between edges. I-UVM-2A follows it (line 1004, falling-edge release). I-UVM-3C then releases reset with a nonblocking assignment at the rising edge, and A-UVM-9 drives a mid-test reset through a clocking block. Both later choices are sound for their synchronous-reset DUTs, and F4C line 683 notes that A-UVM-9's DUT resets synchronously. But neither later lesson says it is refining F4C's rule, so a learner on the route sees three practices with no explanation.
findings.fix: The standard does not decide practice. The facts hold: a drive executed between edges acts at the next clocking event and lands in Re-NBA (IEEE 1800-2023 §14.16). F4C: qualify line 647, for example "So an asynchronous reset stays a direct write; for a DUT with a synchronous reset, a release at the edge with <= or a clocking-block drive is also race-free (I-UVM-3C, A-UVM-9)." I-UVM-3C, at 231: add "F4C releases between edges; with a synchronous reset a nonblocking release at the edge is equally race-free." A-UVM-9, in the rst_if comment or at line 96: add "Safe here because the DUT resets synchronously; F4C explains why an asynchronous reset is written directly."

findings.where: A-UVM-6 line 153 vs I-UVM-2B line 476 (and kata line 1371), A-UVM-7 line 2114, I-UVM-5 line 812, I-SV-5/mailboxes line 325, E-PERF-1 line 265
findings.quotes: A-UVM-6:153 "Predict into a copy, and store items as received." / I-UVM-2B:476 "A scoreboard that stores items for later can clone them as cheap insurance, which is what this site's code style asks for."; A-UVM-7:2114 "scoreboards should also copy before storing"; I-UVM-5:812 "A scoreboard that stores items from a monitor should clone them on entry"
findings.problem: The scoreboard-owning lesson tells learners to store received items uncopied. The TLM owner, the VIP lesson, the container-classes lesson and I-SV-5 tell them to copy before storing, and I-UVM-2B calls that the site's code style. I-UVM-2B's own kata says write_exp() "stores a copy". A-UVM-6's checklist (line 1424) accepts either. Learners get opposite instructions for the same component.
findings.source: The standards do not settle this: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §12.2.10.2 forbids only modifying the received value. Both practices are legal, and I-UVM-2B:476 states the exact condition under which storing a handle uncopied is safe. I found no site style document under docs/ that states the rule, so the course has to choose one.
findings.fix: Pick one site rule and state it the same way everywhere. Recommended: A-UVM-6:153 becomes "Predict into a copy. Storing a received handle is safe only while every publisher creates a new item per transaction (I-UVM-2B, rule 1); clone on entry if you cannot guarantee that." Then either make A-UVM-6's Make It Work clone on store, or soften I-UVM-2B:476 to "can clone them as cheap insurance" without the claim about the site's code style.

findings.where: I-UVM-2B lines 276 and 348 vs A-UVM-6 lines 51, 66, 184-188
findings.quotes: I-UVM-2B:276 "A **predictor** (a component that computes the expected result) feeding a **reference model**"; I-UVM-2B:348 "between analysis-side components: a predictor and a reference model" / A-UVM-6:51 "**Predictor:** the component that turns each observed input into an expected item by calling the reference model"
findings.problem: In I-UVM-2B the predictor computes the expected result and then sends items through a FIFO to a separate reference-model component downstream. In A-UVM-6, the owner of the term, the predictor sits upstream: it calls the reference model, usually a function, and publishes the expected item. I-UVM-2B's wording is also circular: if the predictor already computes the expected result, it is not clear what the downstream model does.
findings.source: Methodology terminology, not settled by IEEE 1800.2-2020. A-UVM-6 is the owner of scoreboards and reference models.
findings.fix: I-UVM-2B:276: "A monitor-side component feeding a transaction-level reference model that consumes time, a model feeding a checker, and two threads inside one component are common examples." I-UVM-2B:348: "a predictor and a time-consuming model it feeds, ...", or drop "predictor" and link A-UVM-6 for the term. A-UVM-6: no change.

findings.where: A-UVM-8 line 518 (Locking an agent's sequencer from a virtual sequence); sequence-arbitration line 274 (lock/grab table) and lines 787-806 (Expert: when is a lock granted?)
findings.quotes: A-UVM-8:518 "`lock()` waits its turn in the arbitration queue; `grab()` goes to the front of it" | sequence-arbitration:274 "It is granted as soon as no other sequence holds a lock or grab."
findings.problem: A-UVM-8 states the simplified reading as fact. I-UVM-3B (sequence-arbitration, plus the lock diagram caption in virtual-sequences and coordinated-attack-lab line 906) teaches that uvm-core 2020.3.1 grants an unblocked lock at once, ahead of older item requests, and that the standard's two clauses disagree. A learner arriving from 3B reads A-UVM-8 as saying the opposite. The link to Sequence Arbitration comes only after the claim.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §14.2.5.5 "arbitrated the same as any other request" vs §15.3.2.10 "after all previously granted requests are completed"; uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_sequencer_base.svh grant_queued_locks() grants the first unblocked lock request at once.
findings.fix: A-UVM-8:518: replace the clause with "`lock()` queues at the back and `grab()` at the front; in uvm-core 2020.3.1 either is granted as soon as no other lock or grab blocks it, and neither takes the sequencer from a current holder or stops the item in flight (see Sequence Arbitration, Expert: when is a lock granted?)", and link that anchor. sequence-arbitration: no change.

findings.where: layered-sequences lines 16 and 99 (definition of atomic sequence); sequence-arbitration line 983; interrupt-handling line 1002; coordinated-attack-lab lines 359 and 908
findings.quotes: layered-sequences:99 "An **atomic sequence** sends exactly one item" | sequence-arbitration:983 "Atomicity needs exclusivity: lock()/unlock() ... Priority never makes a burst atomic."
findings.problem: The same module uses "atomic" in two senses. Layered Sequences defines an "atomic sequence" as a one-item building block, and its scenario sequence of eight atomic writes can be interleaved with other traffic. Sequence Arbitration, Interrupt Handling and the Coordinated Attack lab (with its ATOMIC check) use "atomic" to mean back to back with nothing in between, which needs lock() or grab(). A learner may conclude that a scenario built from atomic sequences is uninterruptible. Layered Sequences never says that it is not.
findings.source: Not a standards term: IEEE 1800.2-2020 defines neither "atomic sequence" nor atomicity for sequences; the exclusivity sense follows §14.2.5.5-§14.2.5.8.
findings.fix: layered-sequences:99: add one sentence: "Atomic here means 'one item, the smallest unit'; it does not mean uninterruptible. Other sequences' items can still be granted between the children of a scenario. To make the scenario back to back, lock the sequencer in the scenario (see Sequence Arbitration, lock() and grab())." Or rename it a "single-item sequence". The other three pages need no change.

findings.where: I-UVM-1D line 992 (interview playground 'one image, many tests', feedback on the +uvm_set_type_override option); I-UVM-1B line 893 (Expert: command line versus code)
findings.quotes: I-UVM-1D:992 "That works in principle, and RNTST then says 'via factory override'" / I-UVM-1B:893 "A command-line override of the test class itself has no effect, because the test already exists when it is applied."
findings.problem: The two lessons disagree on whether +uvm_set_type_override can swap the test. I-UVM-1B is right. In uvm-core 2020.3.1, run_test creates uvm_test_top with create_component_by_name (uvm_root.svh:566) before phasing starts. The override plusargs are applied later, in uvm_root::build_phase through m_do_factory_settings (uvm_root.svh:782). By then the test already exists. The RNTST 'via factory override' message (uvm_root.svh:600) appears only when an override was registered before run_test, for example in tb_top. A learner who believes I-UVM-1D will expect the plusarg to work, and the run will silently use the original test.
findings.source: uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_root.svh: run_test creates the test (line 566) before phasing; build_phase calls m_do_factory_settings (line 782). IEEE 1800.2-2020 G.2.7 defines only the syntax of +uvm_set_type_override, not when it is applied, so the source settles this.
findings.fix: I-UVM-1D:992: change the feedback to: "No. uvm-core applies +uvm_set_type_override in uvm_root's build_phase, after run_test has already created the test, so overriding the test class from the command line does nothing (I-UVM-1B, Expert: command line versus code). Only an override registered in tb_top before run_test changes the test, and RNTST then says 'via factory override'. +UVM_TESTNAME is the tool for this." I-UVM-1B:893: no change.

findings.where: E-PWR-1 line 2008; I-UVM-1C line 902; A-UVM-9 lines 392-393

findings.fix: E-PWR-1:2008: "Against: every component in the domain must be re-entrant. The jump kills the abandoned phase's sequences wherever they are and clears its objections (I-UVM-1C), so drivers and scoreboards must clean up the state those sequences leave behind."

findings.where: I-UVM-2A:84; I-UVM-2B:276; B-AMBA-F1:141; against A-UVM-6:51 and :66 (the owner) and B-AXI-6:50
findings.quotes: I-UVM-2A:84 "A **reference model** or predictor inside the scoreboard computes expected results"; I-UVM-2B:276 "A **predictor** (a component that computes the expected result) feeding a **reference model**"; B-AMBA-F1:141 "A **reference model** (or predictor) computes what the DUT should do" / A-UVM-6:51 "**Predictor:** the component that turns each observed input into an expected item by calling the reference model"; B-AXI-6:50 "a **predictor** is the component that calls it for each observed request"
findings.problem: The owning lesson (A-UVM-6) and B-AXI-6 define two different things. The reference model computes the expected result. The predictor is a separate component, a subscriber outside the scoreboard, that calls the model and publishes expected items. I-UVM-2A and B-AMBA-F1 treat the two words as synonyms, and I-UVM-2A places the predictor inside the scoreboard. I-UVM-2B says the predictor itself computes the expected result and then feeds a reference model through a FIFO, which reverses A-UVM-6's direction. A learner meets I-UVM-2A and I-UVM-2B first, then reads different definitions in A-UVM-6. Spine §5.1 lists 'reference model; predictor (scoreboard)' as separate canonical terms.
findings.fix: I-UVM-2A:84: 'A reference model computes expected results; a predictor is the component that feeds it the observed inputs and passes the expected items to the scoreboard (A-UVM-6).' I-UVM-2B:276: replace the example with 'a predictor feeding expected items to a scoreboard' (or 'a monitor feeding a predictor'), and drop the parenthetical or make it 'a component that calls the reference model'. B-AMBA-F1:141: 'A reference model computes what the DUT should do; a predictor calls it for each observed input'. Line 774 can keep the predictor as a scoreboard method if it notes that this merges the two roles. Glossary concept-terms.ts:739 and :748 already match A-UVM-6.
findings.source: No IEEE clause settles this; it is course terminology. The programme's own rules settle it: spine §5.1 lists 'reference model; predictor (scoreboard)' separately, and A-UVM-6 is the owning lesson. IEEE 1800.2-2020 defines neither term.

Releases it with a direct write between edges ... release it away from the active clock edge." | A-UVM-9:879-889 "a test drives a mid-test reset through cb, so it lands after an edge like every other drive"; "output rst_n; // default output skew 0: updated in Re-NBA" | I-UVM-3C:231 "Reset is released with a nonblocking assignment at a rising edge" | I-SV-4C:702 "##2 cb.rst_n <= 1'b1;"
findings.problem: F4C builds its rule from an asynchronous reset that must change between edges, but its heading and conclusion ('So reset stays a direct write') read as a general rule (I-UVM-2A follows it at line 1004). Later benches do otherwise: five with asynchronous-reset DUTs (I-SV-4B index and local-variables, I-SV-4C, I-SV-7, E-AI-1) list rst_n as a clocking-block output and release it through cb at an edge; I-UVM-3C releases it with <= at the rising edge; A-UVM-9 drives a mid-test reset through a clocking block (its DUT resets synchronously, which F4C line 683 notes). All are deterministic, but none says why it is acceptable or links back to F4C, so a learner sees the opposite of F4C's rule in every later bench. What is inconsistent is the guidance, not a fact.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §14.16 (a drive between edges takes effect 'as if it were executed at the next clocking event'; clocking drives land in Re-NBA); §4.5 (Re-NBA after the active set). Release timing is practice, which F4C itself labels as not a rule of the standard.
findings.fix: F4C: retitle the section 'Asserting an asynchronous reset stays outside the clocking block' and qualify line 647, e.g. "So an asynchronous reset stays a direct write; releasing reset through a clocking block at an edge is deterministic in zero-delay RTL simulation, because the release lands in Re-NBA after that edge's capture (§14.16), and for a DUT with a synchronous reset a release at the edge with <= or a clocking-block drive is also race-free (I-UVM-3C, A-UVM-9)." A-UVM-9 near line 96 or in the rst_if comment: "Safe here because the DUT resets synchronously; F4C explains why an asynchronous reset is written directly." findings.quotes: E-UVM-ML-1:1171 "UVM defines the run-time sub-phases from reset_phase to shutdown_phase in parallel with run_phase." / I-UVM-1C:1208 "twelve run-time phases from pre_reset to post_shutdown"
findings.problem: E-UVM-ML-1 uses 'run-time sub-phases', which spine §5.1 lists as the term not to use, and gives the range as reset_phase to shutdown_phase, narrower than the twelve phases (pre_reset to post_shutdown) in I-UVM-1C, the glossary (concept-terms.ts:553) and the standard.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §9.8.2 'UVM run-time phases' (uvm_pre_reset_phase through uvm_post_shutdown_phase); spine §5.1 'run-time phases' row.
findings.fix: E-UVM-ML-1: replace 'run-time sub-phases' with 'run-time phases' throughout, and at :1166 and :1171 write 'the twelve run-time phases, pre_reset_phase to post_shutdown_phase (IEEE 1800.2-2020 §9.8.2), in parallel with run_phase'. Where the UVM-ML papers' own term is quoted, put it in quotation marks.
